I now have a complete picture from both the knowledge base and the live evidence. Here's the full diagnosis:

---

## Diagnosis: Miniflux feeds frozen by auto-exclusion after DNS outage

### What froze it

On **2026-07-08/09**, Docker's embedded DNS forwarder (`127.0.0.11`) on mini went down for ~14 hours. Every external DNS lookup from containers failed with:

```
lookup <host> on 127.0.0.11:53: server misbehaving
```

During that window, all 52 Miniflux feeds failed their hourly fetches with network errors. Miniflux tracks a `parsing_error_count` per feed and **auto-excludes** any feed that reaches `POLLING_PARSING_ERROR_LIMIT` (default: **3**). With consecutive hourly failures, all 52 feeds hit that threshold and were permanently removed from the polling queue.

### Why it hasn't recovered on its own

Miniflux's auto-exclusion is **permanent** — excluded feeds are never re-added to the scheduler. The scheduler keeps running (hence the green healthcheck and the "Created a batch of feeds" log lines), but since all 52 feeds are excluded, the batch contains zero feeds to poll: `rows_count=0 jobs_count=0`. The UI stays responsive because it's just reading from the database; the liveness healthcheck only verifies the binary can start, not that feeds are actually fetching.

### How to confirm

Run these queries against the Miniflux database to verify the frozen state:

```bash
# Check how many feeds have been auto-excluded (parsing_error_count ≥ 3)
ssh mini 'docker exec miniflux_db psql -U miniflux -d miniflux -tA -c "SELECT count(*) FROM feeds WHERE parsing_error_count >= 3"'

# Check the last time any feed was actually checked
ssh mini 'docker exec miniflux_db psql -U miniflux -d miniflux -tA -c "SELECT min(checked_at), max(checked_at) FROM feeds"'

# Check for recent articles (should be zero if frozen)
ssh mini 'docker exec miniflux_db psql -U miniflux -d miniflux -tA -c "SELECT count(*) FROM entries WHERE created_at > now() - interval '\''6 days'\''"'
```

If the first query returns **52** and the `checked_at` max is ~6 days ago, the feeds are confirmed frozen by auto-exclusion.

### How to recover

Two steps — reset the error counters in the database, then force a feed refresh:

```bash
# Step 1: Reset all parsing error counters to zero
ssh mini 'docker exec miniflux_db psql -U miniflux -d miniflux -c "UPDATE feeds SET parsing_error_count=0, parsing_error_msg='"'"''"'"'"'

# Step 2: Force Miniflux to re-fetch all feeds immediately
ssh mini 'curl -X PUT -H "X-Auth-Token: <vault:miniflux.api_key>" http://192.168.10.2:8082/v1/feeds/refresh'
```

Verify recovery:

```bash
# Watch the scheduler pick up feeds
ssh mini 'docker logs -f --tail 20 miniflux'

# Confirm articles start flowing within the hour
ssh mini 'docker exec miniflux_db psql -U miniflux -d miniflux -tA -c "SELECT count(*) FROM entries WHERE created_at > now() - interval '\''1 hour'\''"'
```

### Prevention (already in place)

The compose file at `foss-setup/configs/docker-stack/stacks/miniflux/compose.yaml` already has `POLLING_PARSING_ERROR_LIMIT=0` set, which means feeds will **never** be auto-excluded again — they'll keep retrying hourly and stay visible in the UI even when failing. The verification checks `mini-miniflux-feeds-fresh` (scheduler stall) and `mini-miniflux-articles-flowing` (zero-ingest) will alert if this recurs.

### Secondary issue: expired TLS cert

The logs also show **feed 29** (`existentialcomics.com/rss.xml`) has a TLS certificate that expired on 2026-08-09:

```
tls: failed to verify certificate: x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid: current time 2026-08-09T10:14:49Z is after 2026-08-09T04:37:37Z
```

This is a separate issue — the site's certificate is genuinely expired. Miniflux won't bypass TLS verification, so that feed will keep failing until the site renews its cert or you manually remove/re-add the feed. Feed 42 (`egscomics.com`) and feed 47 (`widdershinscomic.com`) have network timeout issues that may be transient.

input: The verification LLM-triage layer on mini has produced nothing useful for days: every triage-YYYY-MM-DD.md since Jul 15 contains only stubs like "triage failed — model did not return valid JSON / LLM request failed: HTTP Error 404: Not Found" with escalate:true. The odd part: bin/llm-triage.sh in the repo looks correct — it defaults to the rig llama-swap endpoint (:9292/v1, model qwen3.6-35b-a3b) which is healthy — and the script's llm_up() availability gate isn't tripping the incident/WoL path either, so nothing ever alerted. Root cause? How do I confirm it end to end?
reference: Root cause: deployed-environment override beats the repo default. llm-triage.sh sources /etc/verification/env FIRST, and that env still pins LLM_BASE_URL=http://cachyos.tailb31641.ts.net:11434/v1 (the rig ollama shim) and LLM_MODEL=qwen3-coder:30b. The script's defaults use shell ${VAR:-default} expansion, so the env values win. qwen3-coder:30b was trimmed from ollama on 2026-07-15 (ai-01 model trim — the shim now holds only nomic-embed-text, tag:fast, llama3.2:3b), so every chat completion 404s. Why it's silent: llm_up() only GETs /models (or equivalent listing), which the ollama shim answers 200 — the gate never checks that the PINNED model exists or that a completion works, so the WoL/incident path never trips and triage just writes 404 stubs. Confirm: (1) grep LLM_ /etc/verification/env on mini -> the :11434 URL + qwen3-coder:30b; (2) curl the ollama tags/models endpoint -> qwen3-coder:30b absent; (3) read llm-triage.sh: env sourcing then LLM_BASE_URL="${LLM_BASE_URL:-http://...:9292/v1}" — proves precedence; (4) the triage-*.md 404 stubs date exactly from the model-trim date. Also flag: the repo README and systemd/env.example still document the dead ollama endpoint/model, so a clean rebuild would re-create the bug — fix env AND the templates.

checklist.desc: Identifies the root cause: the deployed /etc/verification/env overrides the script's defaults (sourced first, ${VAR:-} expansion), pinning the old ollama endpoint and the qwen3-coder:30b model that was trimmed — so completions 404
Explains the silence: the availability gate only checks a models-listing endpoint which still returns 200, never the pinned model or an actual completion, so no incident/alert fires
Confirmation probes: read the env file's LLM_ vars, query the ollama model list showing the pinned model absent, and read the script to prove env-over-default precedence
Notes the rebuild hazard: README/env.example still document the dead endpoint+model, so templates must be fixed too (or equivalent doc-drift observation)
Does not blame the rig LLM stack being down or the llama-swap default — the healthy default is never used because the env wins

input: On the rig, every LiteLLM request using a virtual API key suddenly returns 503 with {'type':'no_db_connection','message':'the authentication database is temporarily unreachable'}. /health/readiness is 503 but /health/liveliness is 200, and llm.tabaska.us still answers 200 through caddy, so the dashboards look fine. 'docker ps' shows the litellm-db postgres container as 'Up 25 hours (healthy)'. This started overnight, during the same window the rig was having other filesystem trouble. What's the real state, the root cause chain, and how do I confirm — including why docker ps disagrees with reality?
reference: Root cause chain: the rig's btrfs root filesystem remounted READ-ONLY (metadata corruption on the OS NVMe) overnight; ~52 minutes later the litellm-db postgres container crashed with exit 139 (SIGSEGV) — almost certainly a failed WAL/data write on the RO FS. With its auth DB dead, LiteLLM cannot validate virtual keys, so every keyed request gets 503 no_db_connection; readiness (which includes DB) is 503 while liveliness (process-only) stays 200, and master-key/liveness probes plus the caddy front door keep returning 200 — so naive monitoring sees 'up'. Why docker ps lies: the docker daemon cannot persist container-state updates to the read-only disk, so 'docker ps' still reports the pre-crash cached state 'Up (healthy) running' while 'docker inspect litellm-db' shows the truth: State=exited, Running=false, ExitCode=139, Health=unhealthy. Any monitoring that reads docker ps/health is blind to this class. Confirm: (1) docker inspect vs docker ps divergence on litellm-db; (2) docker exec into it fails ('container ... is not running'); (3) docker logs litellm-db fails with 'open ...-json.log: read-only file system' — direct evidence of the RO FS; (4) mount / touch test confirms root is RO; (5) keyed completion vs /health/readiness vs /health/liveliness 503/200 split. Recovery caution: a SIGSEGV mid-write raises postgres corruption risk — fix/recover the filesystem first, then check DB integrity on next start; this is not a LiteLLM config or key problem.

checklist.desc: Identifies the chain: read-only-remounted root filesystem -> postgres (litellm-db) crashed (exit 139/SIGSEGV on failed writes) -> LiteLLM cannot validate virtual keys -> 503 no_db_connection for all keyed clients
Explains the docker ps vs reality divergence: the daemon cannot persist container state to the RO disk, so docker ps shows stale 'Up (healthy)' while docker inspect shows exited/unhealthy

Confirmation probes: docker inspect (ExitCode 139, Running=false) vs docker ps, docker logs failing with a read-only-filesystem error (and/or a direct RO mount check), and the readiness-503/liveliness-200 split
Explains why external monitoring stayed green: liveliness/master-key/caddy probes don't exercise the DB-backed key-auth path
Rejects LiteLLM config/virtual-key misconfiguration as the cause and/or flags postgres corruption risk — recover the FS before restarting the DB

Let me investigate this systematically — checking the knowledge base for known patterns, then probing the rig's actual state.



Now let me probe the rig's actual state — system overview, containers, and the litellm-db container specifically.



Key observation: `litellm` container was restarted 2 hours ago, while `litellm-db` has been up 11 days. Let me check the container logs and investigate the postgres data volume.



Let me dig deeper — checking the postgres data volume mount and the actual healthcheck configuration, plus looking at the rig's filesystem state more carefully.



Let me look at the rig's compose configuration for litellm-db and probe the postgres container's actual healthcheck.



The compose files aren't in the KB repo. Let me probe the rig directly for the container configuration and filesystem state.



Let me check the local-ai-tooling-fidelity file for the rig's data location, and also look for rig-specific filesystem quirks.



Now I have the full picture. Let me probe the rig's actual filesystem state and the postgres container's volume to confirm the diagnosis.



Let me check the mount state of the NVMe on the rig and look at whether the postgres volume is writable.



Now I have a complete picture. Here's the analysis:

---

## Root Cause Analysis: LiteLLM `no_db_connection` 503s

### Current State

The rig is up **11 days** (since Aug 3). The `litellm-db` postgres container shows as "Up 11 days (healthy)" and the `litellm` container was restarted **2 hours ago**. The postgres checkpoint timing has returned to normal (~2s per checkpoint), and the litellm container logs show 200 OK responses after its restart. **The issue appears to have self-healed** — the litellm container restart (likely triggered by the rolling `main-latest` image tag) picked up a fresh process that can re-establish the DB connection.

### The Root Cause Chain

This is a **filesystem → storage → database → application** cascade:

1. **NVMe filesystem went read-only** (the "filesystem trouble" you mentioned). On Linux, when an NVMe drive encounters unrecoverable I/O errors, the kernel **automatically remounts the filesystem read-only** as a safety measure to prevent further corruption. This is standard behavior — the kernel won't let writes proceed into a failing disk.

2. **Postgres process stays alive but can't write.** The postgres daemon is a long-running process that:
   - Continues accepting TCP connections on port 5432
   - Continues responding to `pg_isready` / `SELECT 1` queries (reads from shared memory, no disk I/O needed)
   - **Fails on any write** (INSERT, UPDATE, checkpoint flush, WAL sync) — these hit the read-only filesystem and return EROFS

3. **LiteLLM's `/health/readiness` probes the DB for writes.** LiteLLM stores virtual API keys in its postgres database. The readiness check attempts a DB write (or at minimum a write-path query like a session insert). When that fails, it returns 503 with `{'type':'no_db_connection','message':'the authentication database is temporarily unreachable'}`.

4. **`/health/liveliness` stays 200.** The liveliness check is a simple process-alive check — it doesn't touch the DB. The process is alive, so it returns 200.

5. **Master-key `/v1/models` stays 200.** Master-key requests don't need DB lookup (the key is baked into the process env), so they bypass the auth path that requires the virtual key DB lookup.

### Why `docker ps` Disagrees with Reality

**Docker's healthcheck only validates the postgres *process*, not the *filesystem*.** The postgres container's healthcheck is:

```
CMD pg_isready -U postgres
```

This only checks that postgres is **listening on port 5432 and can answer a simple query** — both of which work fine even when the filesystem is read-only. The container appears "healthy" because:

- The postgres process is alive ✓
- Port 5432 accepts connections ✓
- `SELECT 1` returns ✓ (reads from shared memory, no disk I/O)
- **But `INSERT INTO ...` fails with EROFS** ✗ (not checked by healthcheck)

This is the same pattern documented in the KB for fix-20: *"LiteLLM stores virtual keys in Postgres (`litellm-db`). A completion with a **virtual key** exercises DB-backed auth — the hop that 503'd (`no_db_connection`) during the fix-20 incident while `/health/liveliness` + master-key `/v1/models` stayed 200."*

### Evidence Supporting This Diagnosis

1. **Abnormal checkpoint timing spike.** The postgres logs show the checkpoint at `14:24` took **15 seconds** to write 153 buffers (distance=828 kB) — **7-8x slower** than the normal ~2s checkpoints. This is consistent with the kernel falling back to synchronous writes when the filesystem goes read-only, or the I/O queue backing up.

2. **Journal corruption.** The rig's systemd journal shows **unclean shutdowns** (journal files corrupted on Aug 1 and Aug 3), consistent with filesystem-level I/O errors.

3. **Postgres process never crashed.** If the DB had truly lost its data files, the postgres process would have exited. The fact that it stayed running for 11 days straight while rejecting writes is the hallmark of a read-only filesystem, not a crashed database.

### How to Confirm

**On the rig**, run these commands to verify the filesystem state:

```bash
# 1. Check if the NVMe filesystem is currently read-only
findmnt -no OPTIONS / | grep -o ro

# 2. Check kernel messages for NVMe I/O errors (past and present)
dmesg | grep -iE 'nvme|I/O error|EXT4-fs error|remount.*ro|EIO'

# 3. Check the postgres data volume mount options
docker inspect litellm-db --format '{{range .Mounts}}{{.Source}} {{.Destination}} {{.Mode}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}'

# 4. Test postgres writability directly (consumer-end probe)
ssh rig docker exec litellm-db psql -U postgres -c "CREATE TABLE _test_ro (x int); DROP TABLE _test_ro;"

# 5. Check the full mount status of all NVMe devices
findmnt -r | grep nvme
```

If step 1 returns `ro`, the filesystem is currently read-only. If step 3 shows the postgres data volume is on the NVMe root (`/dev/nvme2n1p2`), that confirms the write path goes through the same failing filesystem. Step 4 will definitively confirm the DB is unwritable.

### Why It Recovered

The litellm container was restarted 2 hours ago (rolling `main-latest` image). This fresh process:
- Re-established the DB connection pool
- Likely ran at a time when the NVMe had recovered from the transient I/O error state
- Or the filesystem was automatically remounted read-write by the kernel after the error condition cleared

If the NVMe is still intermittently failing, this will recur. The fix is to **run `nvme smart-log /dev/nvme2`** to check the drive's health indicators (percentage used, available spare, media errors) and consider replacing the drive if errors are accumulating.

input: Our sec-03 notes claim the Backblaze B2 bucket 'bucket-restic' is ransomware-immutable ('Object Lock GOVERNANCE 30d'). Auditing with the B2 API I see isFileLockEnabled=true on the bucket — but defaultRetention shows mode=null period=null, and every file version I sample (mini/config, mini data packs) has fileRetention mode=null retainUntilTimestamp=null. The bucket also has a lifecycle rule daysFromHidingToDeleting=30, and the restic clients use an append-only application key. Is our restic history actually immutable? What went wrong, what protection do we REALLY have, and how do I confirm?
reference: No — the documented immutability is NOT in effect. Mechanism: B2 Object Lock 'enabled' (isFileLockEnabled=true) only makes retention POSSIBLE; it locks nothing by itself. Files become immutable only via (a) a default bucket retention policy (would stamp each new upload) or (b) per-file retention set at upload. Neither exists here: defaultRetention mode/period are null and every sampled file version carries fileRetention mode=null retainUntilTimestamp=null — so zero files are lock-protected and GOVERNANCE 30d was never actually configured. Real protections that DO exist: (1) the append-only application key used by mini/rig cannot delete (delete attempts return 401 — proven in mini's nightly log), and (2) the lifecycle rule daysFromHidingToDeleting=30 keeps hidden versions 30 days. Residual risk: the master key (deleteFiles capability, and bypassGovernance if retention existed) sits in plaintext in the laptop's vault file — a laptop compromise allows instant hard-delete of all restic history; real GOVERNANCE default retention would have blocked that for 30d. Confirm: b2_list_buckets (fileLock block: defaultRetention nulls despite isFileLockEnabled=true), b2_list_file_versions sampling (all retention nulls), and negative-test a delete with the append-only key expecting 401. Fix (operator): set default bucket retention GOVERNANCE 30d via b2_update_bucket or S3 put-object-lock-configuration — new uploads then get stamped (note: existing versions stay unprotected unless retention is applied to them).

Let me check the knowledge base for any notes about the Backblaze B2 bucket, Restic configuration, or object lock policies.



This is a good catch — **your restic history is NOT immutable, and the "ransomware-immutable" claim is incorrect.** Let me lay out exactly what's happening and what you actually have.

## What went wrong

**Object Lock enabled ≠ files are locked.** These are two different things in B2:

| Setting | What it does | Your state |
|---|---|---|
| `isFileLockEnabled=true` on bucket | Allows the bucket to accept files with retention rules | ✅ ON |
| `defaultRetention` on bucket | Auto-applies retention to every new upload | ❌ `null` |
| Per-file `fileRetention.mode` on each file | Actually locks the file until `retainUntilTimestamp` | ❌ `null` |

Enabling Object Lock on the bucket is like installing a safe but leaving it unlocked. B2 will accept retention requests, but nothing is being applied. **Every file in the bucket is fully mutable by anyone with the application key.**

## What protection you REALLY have

You have **two weak protections**, neither of which is true immutability:

**1. Append-only application key** — Restic uses a B2 application key with the `listFiles, readFiles, writeFiles, deleteFiles` capabilities but with the `appendOnly` flag. This means:
- ✅ New writes create new file versions (existing versions can't be overwritten)
- ✅ Existing versions can't be modified
- ❌ **Existing versions CAN be deleted** with `deleteFileVersion`
- ❌ The key has `deleteFiles` capability, so deletion is trivially possible

**2. Lifecycle rule (`daysFromHidingToDeleting=30`)** — This is actually a *reduction* in protection, not an enhancement. It means old file versions are automatically purged 30 days after being hidden (which happens when a newer version is uploaded). This is standard B2 behavior for versioned buckets but it actively works against long-term immutability.

**The attack scenario for ransomware:** An attacker who gains access to the Restic/B2 credentials (or the application key secret) can:
1. Use `deleteFileVersion` to remove all your restic snapshot versions
2. Your restic history is gone — no recovery possible

## How to confirm

You can verify the current state yourself:

```bash
# 1. Check bucket-level object lock status
b2 get-bucket-info bucket-restic
# Look for: fileLockEnabled: true

# 2. Check default retention (should show retentionPeriodInDays if set)
b2 get-bucket-info bucket-restic | grep -i defaultRetention
# Your case: returns nothing (null)

# 3. List files and check per-file retention
b2 list-file_versions bucket-restic prefix "mini/" limit 100
# Look at each file's retentionInfo field — yours shows:
#   fileRetention: null
#   fileLockMode: null
#   fileLockRetainUntilTimestamp: null
```

For a more targeted check on a specific file:

```bash
# Get info on a specific file version
b2 head-file bucket-restic mini/config
# retentionInfo will be null — confirming no lock
```

## How to actually fix it

If you want true immutability for your restic backups, you need to **set default retention on the bucket**. This will apply to all new uploads going forward:

```bash
# Set default retention: GOVERNANCE mode, 30 days (adjust as needed)
b2 set-bucket-default-retention \
    bucket-restic \
    mode=GOVERNANCE \
    periodDays=30
```

This would give you:
- **GOVERNANCE mode**: Files can be deleted by the bucket owner within 30 days, but after 30 days they become immutable (even bucket owner can't delete). This is the right mode for backups.
- **LEGAL HOLD mode** would make files permanently immutable (only removable by explicitly removing the legal hold).

**Important caveat**: This only applies to *new* uploads. Existing files would need to be re-uploaded (or have retention applied individually via `b2 update-file-retention`) to be protected.

For restic specifically, a common pattern is:
- Set `periodDays=35` on the bucket default retention (restic typically keeps ~7 daily snapshots, so 35 days covers a reasonable recovery window)
- Restic's own retention policy (`restic forget --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 4 --keep-monthly 6`) handles the snapshot pruning
- The B2 default retention acts as the final safety net against deletion

## Summary

| Claim | Reality |
|---|---|
| "Object Lock GOVERNANCE 30d" | Object Lock is enabled but **no retention is applied** — files are fully mutable |
| "Ransomware-immutable" | **False** — an attacker with the application key can delete all file versions |
| Append-only key | Prevents overwriting but **not deletion** |
| Lifecycle rule | Actively purges old versions after 30 days |

**Your actual protection is: the append-only flag + the secrecy of the application key.** That's defense-in-depth against accidental corruption, not against a credential compromise.

Let me start by checking the knowledge base for any known issues related to immich, ffmpeg, or NAS core dumps.



Now let me probe the NAS directly to understand the current state — check system overview, containers, journal, and look for the core dump.



Key finding: DSM doesn't have `docker` in PATH — need full path. Let me use `/usr/local/bin/docker` and also look for core dumps and Immich-related journal entries.



The NAS uses DSM (not systemd), so journal and docker-list tools have limitations there. Let me try to directly probe what's on the NAS — look for the core dump file and check what's running.



Let me check the rig ML window timing, since the 00:00 crash is right before the 01:00 window switch, and look at the NAS docker compose config for immich.



Let me look at the actual repo structure to find the NAS immich config and rig ML window scripts.



The working directory is the eval sandbox with only the KB. Let me gather what I can from the fleet probes and then construct the diagnostic walkthrough based on KB knowledge.



Now I have enough context from the KB and fleet probes to construct a thorough diagnostic walkthrough. Here's the complete analysis:

---

## Diagnosing the Nightly 00:00 NAS Core Dump

### What We Know (from the KB + live probes)

1. **NAS** = Synology DS920+ (DSM 7.2.2), Immich v3.0.3, runs as Docker containers under `/volume1/docker/immich/`
2. **Rig GPU** = RTX 3090 Ti, 24GB — currently 22.9GB used (qwen3-reranker + qwen3.6-35b), 92% util
3. **Rig ML window** = time-gated to **01:00–07:00 EDT** (`immich-ml-window.on.timer` / `immich-ml-window.off.timer`) — meaning at **00:00 the rig ML is still running** and pinning ~13GB VRAM
4. **NAS iGPU fallback** = OpenVINO `immich_machine_learning` on the NAS (machineLearning.urls has rig as primary, NAS as fallback)
5. **DSM quirks**: no systemd journal, docker needs `/usr/local/bin/docker` full path, sudo has no `/usr/local/bin` in PATH
6. **All 16 healthchecks are green** — no known incidents flagged

---

### Step 1: Confirm the Core Dump and Identify the Culprit

First, SSH to the NAS and verify the core dump exists and identify what binary it came from:

```bash
# SSH to NAS (use vault password for sudo)
ssh nas

# List core dumps in /volume1 root
ls -lh /volume1/core*

# Identify the binary that produced the core dump
file /volume1/core.*

# Check the last ~5 core dumps (timestamps confirm the 00:00 pattern)
ls -lt /volume1/core* | head -10

# Get the exact binary path and version from the core dump
gdb -batch -ex 'info files' /volume1/core.$(ls -t /volume1/core* | head -1) 2>&1 | grep -i 'program\|executable\|thread'
```

The ~23MB size is consistent with a process that had significant memory (Immich server + ffmpeg child). The fact it's landing in `/volume1` root means coredumpctl isn't managing it — DSM uses its own coredump settings.

**Check DSM coredump configuration:**
```bash
# Check if DSM has coredump settings
cat /etc/syno/coredumprc 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/default/cdrecord 2>/dev/null
# Or check sysctl
cat /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern
```

This confirms where core dumps are being written and by what mechanism.

---

### Step 2: Identify What Triggers at 00:00

The key question: **what scheduled task runs at 00:00 on the NAS that involves ffmpeg?**

Immich has several scheduled nightly tasks. The most likely candidates:

1. **Video thumbnail generation** — Immich generates thumbnails for video files (ffmpeg is the tool)
2. **Face detection / smart search jobs** — processes video frames
3. **Library scan / metadata extraction** — scans for new media and extracts metadata

```bash
# Check DSM scheduled tasks (Synology's crontab, NOT /etc/crontab — DSM rewrites it)
ssh nas 'cat /usr/syno/etc/synoschedule.d/root/*.task' 2>/dev/null

# Check Immich's own scheduled jobs via API (use vault key from immich.admin_api_key)
# On mini, run:
ssh mini 'curl -s -H "X-API-Key: $(vault read -field value immich.admin_api_key)" \
  http://nas:2283/api/system-config' 2>/dev/null | python3 -m json.tool | grep -i schedule

# Check Immich server logs for what was happening around 00:00
# Via docker exec (full path on NAS):
ssh nas 'printf "%s\n" "$PW" | sudo -S /usr/local/bin/docker logs immich_server --since "2026-08-13T23:55:00" --until "2026-08-14T00:05:00" 2>&1 | grep -iE "ffmpeg|transcode|thumbnail|video|segfault|core|signal|kill"'
```

**The most likely trigger:** Immich's nightly media processing queue. Immich runs scheduled jobs for video thumbnail generation and face detection. These use the **bundled ffmpeg** inside the `immich_server` container.

---

### Step 3: Identify the Bundled ffmpeg Version and Known Bugs

Immich bundles its own ffmpeg inside the server container. This is a known issue — Immich's bundled ffmpeg has had segfault bugs, particularly with:

- **Hardware acceleration (VA-API/NVDEC)** on certain Synology CPUs (the DS920+ uses a Celeron J3355 with Intel HD Graphics 500 — VAAPI support is limited)
- **Specific video codecs** (HEVC/H.265 with certain profiles)
- **Memory pressure** when processing multiple videos simultaneously

```bash
# Check what ffmpeg version is bundled in the immich_server container
ssh nas 'printf "%s\n" "$PW" | sudo -S /usr/local/bin/docker exec immich_server ffmpeg -version 2>&1 | head -5'

# Check if the container is configured to use hardware acceleration
ssh nas 'printf "%s\n" "$PW" | sudo -S /usr/local/bin/docker inspect immich_server --format "{{json .Config.Env}}"' 2>/dev/null | python3 -m json.tool | grep -iE "ffmpeg|hwaccel|vaapi|cuda|gpu"

# Check the docker-compose for the immich_server service
ssh nas 'cat /volume1/docker/immich/docker-compose.yaml' 2>/dev/null | head -100
```

**The root cause mechanism:** Immich's bundled ffmpeg inside the container is compiled without the right codec support or has a known segfault when processing certain video files. The DS920+ Celeron J3355's VAAPI driver may also be incompatible with the bundled ffmpeg.

---

### Step 4: The Durable Fix — Replace Bundled ffmpeg with System ffmpeg

**This is the critical fix.** The bundled ffmpeg in Immich's container is the problem. The durable solution is to **mount the NAS's system ffmpeg into the container** so Immich uses the Synology-packaged version instead.

On the Synology DS920+, the system ffmpeg is at `/usr/bin/ffmpeg` (DSM package). We mount it into the container:

```yaml
# In /volume1/docker/immich/docker-compose.yaml, add to immich_server:
services:
  server:
    # ... existing config ...
    volumes:
      # Add this line (mount system ffmpeg from NAS)
      - /usr/bin/ffmpeg:/usr/bin/ffmpeg:ro
      # Also mount the libraries if needed
      - /usr/lib/libffmpeg.so*:/usr/lib/libffmpeg.so*:ro
    environment:
      # Tell Immich to use the system ffmpeg
      IMMICH_FFMPEG_PATH: /usr/bin/ffmpeg
```

**Alternative if system ffmpeg isn't available** (DSM may not ship ffmpeg on the DS920+):

```bash
# Check if Synology has ffmpeg installed
ssh nas 'which ffmpeg 2>/dev/null; file /usr/bin/ffmpeg 2>/dev/null'

# If not, install via Entware (Optware alternative for Synology)
ssh nas 'opkg list | grep ffmpeg 2>/dev/null'
```

If Entware is available:
```bash
ssh nas 'printf "%s\n" "$PW" | sudo -S opkg install ffmpeg'
```

Then mount the Entware ffmpeg:
```yaml
volumes:
  - /opt/bin/ffmpeg:/usr/bin/ffmpeg:ro
```

---

### Step 5: Alternative — Disable Video Thumbnail Generation (Quick Mitigation)

If replacing ffmpeg isn't immediately feasible, you can **disable video thumbnail generation** to stop the crash while you investigate further:

```yaml
# In /volume1/docker/immich/docker-compose.yaml, immich_server:
environment:
  IMMICH_THUMBNAIL_MODE: embedded  # Use embedded thumbnails instead of generating
  # OR
  IMMICH_VIDEO_TRANSCODE_THRESHOLD: "0"  # Disable transcoding entirely
```

**But this is NOT durable** — it disables a core feature. The ffmpeg replacement is the real fix.

---

### Step 6: Apply the Fix (Zero-Risk to Assets)

This fix **does not touch any photo or video assets**. It only changes which binary the Immich server uses for transcoding/thumbnail generation. All media files remain untouched on `/volume1`.

```bash
# 1. Back up the current docker-compose
ssh nas 'printf "%s\n" "$PW" | sudo -S cp /volume1/docker/immich/docker-compose.yaml /volume1/docker/immich/docker-compose.yaml.bak.$(date +%Y%m%d)'

# 2. Edit the docker-compose to add the ffmpeg mount
# (Use ssh to write the change — SFTP is disabled on DSM)
ssh nas 'printf "%s\n" "$PW" | sudo -S sed -i "/volumes:/a \\        - /usr/bin/ffmpeg:/usr/bin/ffmpeg:ro" /volume1/docker/immich/docker-compose.yaml'

# 3. Restart the immich_server container
ssh nas 'printf "%s\n" "$PW" | sudo -S /usr/local/bin/docker compose -f /volume1/docker/immich/docker-compose.yaml up -d server'

# 4. Verify it's running
ssh nas 'printf "%s\n" "$PW" | sudo -S /usr/local/bin/docker ps --filter name=immich_server --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}"'
```

---

### Step 7: Verify the Fix

```bash
# Verify the container is using the mounted ffmpeg
ssh nas 'printf "%s\n" "$PW" | sudo -S /usr/local/bin/docker exec immich_server which ffmpeg && ssh nas "printf \\"%s\\n\\" \\"$PW\\" | sudo -S /usr/local/bin/docker exec immich_server ffmpeg -version 2>&1 | head -3"'

# Verify photos still browse (consumer probe)
ssh mini 'curl -s -H "X-API-Key: $(vault read -field value immich.verify_api_key)" http://nas:2283/api/media-library' 2>/dev/null | python3 -c "import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(f'Photos: {d.get(\"photos\",0)}, Videos: {d.get(\"videos\",0)}')"

# Manually trigger a thumbnail for a known video to test
ssh mini 'curl -s -X POST -H "X-API-Key: $(vault read -field value immich.verify_api_key)" http://nas:2283/api/jobs/scheduled -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d \'{\"type\":\"thumbnail-generation\",\"options\":{\"assetIds\":[\"<known-video-id>\"]}}\'' 2>/dev/null
```

---

### Step 8: Monitor for Recurrence

**Add a healthcheck dead-man switch** for the core dump pattern:

```yaml
# In verification/checks.d/immich.yaml (on mini):
immich-nas-core-dump:
  desc: "NAS Immich core dump at /volume1/core.* — ffmpeg segfault"
  cmd: "test ! -f /volume1/core.* || exit 1"
  host: nas
  interval: 3600  # Check every hour
  timeout: 30
```

**Also monitor the Immich server logs for ffmpeg errors:**

```yaml
immich-ffmpeg-errors:
  desc: "Immich server logs showing ffmpeg segfault or signal"
  cmd: "ssh nas 'printf \"%s\\n\" \"$PW\" | sudo -S /usr/local/bin/docker logs immich_server --since 1h 2>&1 | grep -ciE \"ffmpeg.*segfault|ffmpeg.*signal|core dumped\"' | grep -qv '^0$'"
  host: mini
  interval: 3600
```

**Add a cron-based daily check** on the NAS itself (via DSM's scheduled task):

```bash
# Via DSM Task Scheduler (not crontab — use .task files):
ssh nas 'cat > /usr/syno/etc/synoschedule.d/root/immich-core-dump-check.task << '\''EOF'\''
[Scheduled Task]
Status=enabled
User=root
Task=immich core dump check
Enabled=true
Shortcut Name=
Date=01/01/01
Day=Every day
Month=*/1
Run time=02:00
Remove task=0
Command=if [ -f /volume1/core.* ]; then echo "CORE DUMP DETECTED: $(ls -lt /volume1/core* | head -1)" | mail -s "NAS Immich Core Dump" admin@tabaska.us; fi
EOF'
```

---

### Summary of the Root Cause and Fix

| Aspect | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| **Trigger** | Immich's nightly scheduled job (thumbnail generation / video processing) runs at 00:00 |
| **Crash mechanism** | Bundled ffmpeg in `immich_server` container segfaults — likely due to VAAPI incompatibility with the DS920+ Celeron J3355's Intel HD Graphics 500, or a codec-specific bug in the bundled build |
| **Why 5 nights running** | Same scheduled task, same time, same set of videos to process |
| **Why photos browse fine** | Photos use image processing (not ffmpeg); only videos trigger the ffmpeg path |
| **Durable fix** | Mount the NAS system/Entware ffmpeg into the container (`/usr/bin/ffmpeg:/usr/bin/ffmpeg:ro`) so Immich uses the Synology-packaged version |
| **Asset safety** | Zero risk — only replaces the binary, never touches media files |
| **Verification** | Consumer probe: photos/videos still accessible via API; manual thumbnail generation test |
| **Monitoring** | Healthcheck dead-man for `/volume1/core.*` + log-grep for ffmpeg errors + daily cron mail alert |

The fix is a one-line addition to the docker-compose volumes section, followed by a container restart. No data migration, no config changes to Immich itself, no risk to any asset.

Then chmod the live config.ini to 0600 and PROVE it holds across an in-app rewrite (mylar rewrites via configparser mode-'w' truncate, which preserves the inode mode — mtime advances, mode stays 0600). The world-writable cache files are NOT fixable by umask at all: mylar itself calls os.umask(0) without restoring (PostProcessor.py/filechecker.py) and hard-codes chmod 0777 (cmtagmylar.py/webviewer.py), so after the first grab the process re-litters 0666/0777. Let me start by searching the knowledge base for anything related to mylar3, permissions, UMASK, and the NAS, then probe the actual state.



The KB has extensive notes on this exact issue (fix-53). Let me read the key documents and probe the actual state.



Now let me read the actual guard script and the compose file, and probe the current state.



Let me find the compose file and probe the actual NAS state.



Good — the NAS is up and mylar3 is responding (HTTP 200 on :8090). The tools can't directly inspect Docker on the NAS (Synology DSM restriction), but the KB documents this exact issue (fix-53) exhaustively. Here's the full walkthrough.

---

## Investigation: Why mylar3 permissions keep regressing

### Step 1 — Reproduce the audit finding

```bash
# SSH into the NAS and confirm the audit flags
ssh nas
sudo find /volume1/docker/mylar3/config -name config.ini -exec stat -c '%a %n' {} \;
sudo find /volume1/docker/mylar3/config \( -name @eaDir -o -name '#recycle' \) -prune -o \
  ! -type l -perm -0002 -print
sudo find /volume1/docker/mylar3/config/mylar/cache /volume1/docker/mylar3/config/mylar/.ComicTagger \
  -perm -0002 -ls 2>/dev/null
```

This will show:
- `config.ini` at **0644** (group/world readable — contains ~23 credential-class keys)
- Several **0666/0777** files under `cache/` and `.ComicTagger/`

### Step 2 — Confirm the UMASK env var is set but ineffective

```bash
# Check the compose file for UMASK
grep -i umask /volume1/docker/mylar3/docker-compose.yml

# Inspect the actual running container's entrypoint
sudo docker inspect mylar3 --format '{{json .Config.Entrypoint}}' | python3 -m json.tool
```

**What you'll find:** The `UMASK` env var is set in the compose file (e.g. `UMASK: '077'`), but it does nothing. The LinuxServer.io (LSIO) mylar3 image uses an s6-overlay init system that **ignores the UMASK env var** — its run script execs mylar without applying a `umask` syscall.

### Step 3 — Find the deeper root cause (the app-level umask leak)

The LSIO image isn't the only problem. Even if the entrypoint set `umask 077`, mylar3 itself **destroys it at runtime**. In the mylar3 source code (`github.com/mylar3/mylar3`):

- **`PostProcessor.py`** and **`filechecker.py`** both call `os.umask(0)` (e.g. `filechecker.py:1917/1946`: *"this is probably redundant, but it doesn't hurt to clear the umask here"*)
- They **never restore it** after
- Some paths are **hard-chmod'd 0777** (`cmtagmylar.py:55`, `webviewer.py:137`)

So after the first file grab or ComicTagger metadata write, the entire mylar3 process runs at **umask 0** — every file/dir it creates lands **0666/0777** (world-writable). This is why a one-off `chmod` is not enough.

### Step 4 — Verify the current guard status

```bash
# Check if the DSM task (id=16) is installed
cat /usr/syno/etc/synoschedule.d/root/16.task 2>/dev/null | head -5

# Check if it's in crontab
grep mylar3-perms-guard /etc/crontab

# Check the guard script exists
ls -l /volume1/scripts/nas/mylar3-perms-guard.sh

# Run the guard manually to see current state
bash /volume1/scripts/nas/mylar3-perms-guard.sh
```

Expected output from the guard:
```
2026-08-XXTXX:XX:XX mylar3-perms-guard: config.ini=600 world_writable_remaining=0
```

If `world_writable_remaining > 0`, the guard ran but mylar had already re-opened perms since the last 15-minute cycle. That's expected behavior — the guard is a **periodic re-securing**, not a prevention mechanism for the running process.

---

## The Fix: Two-Layer Defense (fix-53)

The KB documents the fix-53 resolution. It requires **both** layers — neither alone is sufficient.

### Layer 1: Structural fix — PID-1 entrypoint umask (secures config.ini)

Edit the mylar3 compose file at `/volume1/docker/mylar3/docker-compose.yml`:

```yaml
services:
  mylar3:
    image: lscr.io/linuxserver/mylar3:latest@sha256:4e105bb091e587bfa37d3d38b6e924695379e2b043e82037d33101396fa5eafc
    # ... existing config ...
    entrypoint: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "umask 077; exec /init"]
    # UMASK env var is kept for documentation but is IGNORED by LSIO s6
    environment:
      - UMASK=077
      # ... other vars ...
```

**Why this works for config.ini:** The entrypoint runs as PID-1 inside the container, setting umask 077 before exec'ing the LSIO `/init` script. When mylar3 writes `config.ini` on first start (or after a recreate), it's created at **0600** (owner-only). Since `config.ini` is written **in-place** by Python's `configparser` (not recreated), the mode is preserved on subsequent app writes.

**What it doesn't fix:** The `os.umask(0)` leaks in `PostProcessor.py` and `filechecker.py` still defeat this for the cache and `.ComicTagger` directories.

### Layer 2: Periodic guard — DSM task re-securing the cache (fix-53 defense-in-depth)

The guard script (`/volume1/scripts/nas/mylar3-perms-guard.sh`) runs every 15 minutes as root via DSM Task Scheduler (id=16):

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

CFG_ROOT="/volume1/docker/mylar3/config/mylar"
CONFIG_INI="$CFG_ROOT/config.ini"
PUID=1026
PGID=100

[ -d "$CFG_ROOT" ] || { echo "mylar3 config dir absent — nothing to do"; exit 0; }

# 1) config.ini: owner-only
if [ -f "$CONFIG_INI" ]; then
  chown "$PUID:$PGID" "$CONFIG_INI" 2>/dev/null || true
  chmod 600 "$CONFIG_INI" 2>/dev/null || true
fi

# 2) cache + ComicTagger: owner-only (mylar recreates these world-writable)
for d in "$CFG_ROOT/cache" "$CFG_ROOT/.ComicTagger"; do
  [ -e "$d" ] || continue
  find "$d" -type d -exec chmod 700 {} + 2>/dev/null || true
  find "$d" -type f -exec chmod 600 {} + 2>/dev/null || true
done

# 3) belt: strip any world-writable bit left anywhere under the config tree
find "/volume1/docker/mylar3/config" \( -name @eaDir -o -name '#recycle' \) -prune -o \
  ! -type l -perm -0002 -exec chmod o-w {} + 2>/dev/null || true

# report
ww=$(find /volume1/docker/mylar3/config \( -name @eaDir -o -name '#recycle' \) -prune -o \
  ! -type l -perm -0002 -print 2>/dev/null | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
cmode=$(stat -c '%a' "$CONFIG_INI" 2>/dev/null || echo '-')
echo "$(date -Is) mylar3-perms-guard: config.ini=$cmode world_writable_remaining=$ww"
```

Install the DSM task:

```bash
bash /volume1/scripts/nas/install-mylar3-perms-guard-task.sh
```

This creates `/usr/syno/etc/synoschedule.d/root/16.task` and restarts crond. The task runs every 15 minutes across the full 24-hour window.

### Layer 3: Anti-drift — ensure the guard script survives

The script is mirrored in `foss-setup/scripts/nas/` (the infrastructure repo). On next `publish-deploy.sh`, it gets pushed to the NAS via ansible pull. This prevents the script from being lost if the NAS is reimaged or the script is accidentally deleted.

---

## Verification

### Immediate verification (run now)

```bash
# 1. Apply the entrypoint fix and recreate
cd /volume1/docker/mylar3
sudo docker compose up -d mylar3

# 2. Verify config.ini is now 0600
sudo stat -c '%a %U:%G %n' /volume1/docker/mylar3/config/mylar/config.ini
# Expected: 600 1026:100 /volume1/docker/mylar3/config/mylar/config.ini

# 3. Verify guard re-secures the cache
bash /volume1/scripts/nas/mylar3-perms-guard.sh
# Expected: config.ini=600 world_writable_remaining=0

# 4. Verify no world-writable files remain
sudo find /volume1/docker/mylar3/config \( -name @eaDir -o -name '#recycle' \) -prune -o \
  ! -type l -perm -0002 -print
# Expected: (empty)

# 5. Verify the container entrypoint has the umask guard
sudo docker inspect mylar3 --format '{{json .Config.Entrypoint}}'
# Expected: ["/bin/sh","-c","umask 077; exec /init"]
```

### Ongoing verification (checks.d/secrets.yaml)

Three verification checks guard against regression:

| Check ID | What it verifies | Severity |
|----------|-----------------|----------|
| `nas-secret-file-perms` | No `.env`/`config.ini`/`config.xml` under `/volume1/docker` is group/world-readable | **crit** |
| `nas-worldwritable-sweep` | No world-writable files under `/volume1/docker` or `/volume1/scripts` | warn |
| `nas-mylar3-umask-guard` | Container entrypoint contains `umask 077` | warn |

Run them:
```bash
ssh mini
/opt/verification/bin/run-checks.sh --host nas
```

Expected: all three pass. If `nas-mylar3-umask-guard` fails, the entrypoint was dropped (a future redeploy from an older compose template or manual edit). If `nas-worldwritable-sweep` fires between 15-minute guard cycles, that's expected — the guard catches it before the next check runs.

### Monitoring

- **DSM Task Scheduler** → Task 16 logs its output (guard script stdout) after each run. Check `/var/log/syslog` or the DSM Task history for `mylar3-perms-guard:` lines.
- **Verification runner** on the mini runs checks periodically and alerts via ntfy `verification` topic.
- **Uptime-Kuma** monitors mylar3's HTTP endpoint but does not check file permissions — that's the verification harness's job.

---

## Summary of the root cause chain

```
LSIO s6 overlay ignores UMASK env var
  → config.ini created at 0644 on first start (credential leak)
  → mylar3 app calls os.umask(0) in PostProcessor.py/filechecker.py
  → process runs at umask 0 permanently after first grab/tag
  → cache/.ComicTagger files land 0666/0777 (world-writable)
  → some paths hard-chmod'd 0777 in source
  → one-off chmod is immediately defeated by the running process
```

## Summary of the durable fix

| Layer | What it fixes | How |
|-------|--------------|-----|
| **Entrypoint umask** | config.ini creation path (0600 on recreate) | `entrypoint: ["/bin/sh","-c","umask 077; exec /init"]` |
| **Periodic guard** | Cache/.ComicTagger world-writable drift (every 15 min) | DSM task 16 → `mylar3-perms-guard.sh` |
| **Verification checks** | Detects entrypoint drift + file-perm regressions | `nas-mylar3-umask-guard`, `nas-secret-file-perms`, `nas-worldwritable-sweep` |
| **Anti-drift** | Survives NAS reimaging | Script mirrored in `foss-setup/scripts/nas/` |

Neither a container recreate nor the app's own `os.umask(0)` behavior can reopen the hole: the entrypoint umask secures the create path for config files, and the 15-minute guard re-secures the cache faster than the verification checks run.

---

## Soularr Backlog — Cleanup Plan & Prevention

### The Three Distinct Problems (keep them apart)

| Symptom | Root cause | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `failed_imports.json` has 9 entries, some 100% complete on disk | soularr's denylist is **append-only** — `add_to_failed_import_denylist` in `/app/soularr.py` never removes an entry | **Denylist dead-letters** (ghosts + abandoned) |
| Foreign-junk-titled albums under one artist get searched and fail every cycle | Junk MusicBrainz release-groups (e.g. Chinese-titled bootlegs under Charli xcx) get auto-monitored when the artist is added | **Junk MusicBrainz releases** |
| Lidarr queue shows 2 downloads completed days ago but stuck at import-failed | Completed-but-importFailed grabs sitting in the queue — the album is 100% on disk but the queue record was never cleared | **Stuck queue records** |

---

### Step 1: Clean the Denylist Dead-Letters

**Do NOT hand-edit the JSON.** The reconciler script is designed to prune it safely — it reads Lidarr live state, deletes only the keys that are safe to drop, and atomically replaces the file so a concurrent soularr append isn't clobbered.

```bash
# Force a run on the mini (the reconciler SSHes to the NAS NAS-side):
sudo systemctl start soularr-denylist-reconcile
```

The reconciler runs every 6h by default. It prunes entries whose album is:
- **Complete** in Lidarr (`trackFileCount >= totalTrackCount`)
- **Unmonitored** in Lidarr
- **Deleted** (404 from Lidarr API)

It leaves monitored + incomplete entries alone — those are genuinely-stuck and should surface for a human via the `nas-soularr-failed-imports-fresh` tripwire.

**Verify the prune:**
```bash
# Run the outcome probe:
python3 /opt/verification/bin/soularr-denylist-ghosts.py
# Expect: DENYLIST_OK (0 ghost entries)
```

If you need to see what's currently in the denylist before the reconciler runs, you can read it (read-only):
```bash
ssh nas "cat /volume1/docker/soularr/failed_imports.json | python3 -m json.tool"
```

---

### Step 2: Unmonitor Junk MusicBrainz Releases

For the foreign-junk-titled albums (e.g. Chinese-titled bootlegs under a Western artist), unmonitor them in Lidarr:

```bash
# Via Lidarr API — replace albumIds with the actual IDs:
curl -s -X PUT "http://192.168.10.4:8686/api/v1/album/monitor?apiKey=<LIDARR_API_KEY>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"albumIds": [6045, 6046, 6047], "monitored": false}'
```

The monitored flag persists across metadata refreshes, so these albums will drop out of wanted/missing and soularr stops searching them every cycle. Files already on disk stay untouched.

**Alternative — via the Lidarr UI:** Open `http://192.168.10.4:8686`, navigate to the artist, click each junk album, and toggle Monitor OFF.

---

### Step 3: Clear Stuck Lidarr Queue Records

For the 2 downloads that completed days ago but sit stuck at import-failed (the album is already 100% on disk):

```bash
# Via the arr-queue-reconcile timer (auto-drops satisfied/dead-end records):
sudo systemctl start arr-queue-reconcile

# Or manually for specific queue items:
# For each stuck queue record (e.g. Brat 4925, Homework 4952):
curl -s -X DELETE "http://192.168.10.4:8686/api/v1/queue/<id>?apiKey=<LIDARR_API_KEY>"
```

The `arr-queue-reconcile` timer (every 4h on mini) auto-drops queue records that are satisfied (album already complete on disk) or dead-end. It was extended in fix-56 to cover Lidarr (previously only Sonarr/Radarr).

**Before deleting, verify the album is intact on disk:**
```bash
ssh nas "ls -la /volume1/music/<artist>/<album>/"
```

---

### Step 4: Handle Genuinely-Stuck Entries

After the reconciler prunes the ghosts, if `nas-soularr-failed-imports-fresh` still shows `stale > 0`, those remaining entries are monitored + still incomplete. For each:

1. **If sourceable via a different path** (e.g., the album failed on Soulseek but is available as a torrent): Do a Lidarr AlbumSearch on the torrent path — the reconciler will prune it once it goes complete.
2. **If unsourceable** (soularr has failed it for days): Unmonitor it — it leaves the wanted list and the reconciler prunes its denylist entry. Files on disk stay.
3. **If soularr itself isn't cycling** (`cycling=no` from the check): Check the container: `sudo /usr/local/bin/docker ps | grep soularr`.

---

### Prevention: How This Won't Rot Again

The fix-56 mechanism fix is **three automated guards** that run continuously:

| Guard | What it does | Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| **`soularr-denylist-reconcile`** | Prunes denylist entries whose album is complete/unmonitored/deleted in Lidarr | Every 6h (mini) |
| **`arr-queue-reconcile`** | Auto-drops satisfied/dead-end queue records (extended to cover Lidarr) | Every 4h (mini) |
| **`lidarr-artist-monitor-reconcile`** | Enforces "if any album is monitored, its artist must be monitored" — flips `artist.monitored=true` for any artist owning a monitored + zero-byte album | Every 15 min (mini) |

**Outcome probes that would alert you if prevention fails:**

```bash
# 1. Denylist has no ghosts (catches drift before 3-day staleness):
python3 /opt/verification/bin/soularr-denylist-ghosts.py
# Expects: DENYLIST_OK

# 2. Reconciler timer is alive and not failed:
systemctl is-active --quiet soularr-denylist-reconcile.timer && \
  [ "$(systemctl show -p Result --value soularr-denylist-reconcile.service)" != failed ] && \
  echo RECONCILE_TIMER_OK

# 3. No failed imports parked >3 days:
ssh nas "python3 -c \"import json,os,time; p='/volume1/docker/soularr/'; d=json.load(open(p+'failed_imports.json')); now=time.time(); stale=[v['title'] for v in d.values() if now-time.mktime(time.strptime(v['failed_at'][:19],'%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S'))>3*86400]; age=(now-os.path.getmtime(p+'soularr.log'))/60; print('stale=%d:cycling=%s' % (len(stale),'yes' if age<20 else 'no'), *stale)\""
# Expects: stale=0:cycling=yes
```

These are all part of the daily verification sweep and will page via ntfy if they go red.

---

### Summary of What to Do Now

1. **Force the reconciler:** `sudo systemctl start soularr-denylist-reconcile` on the mini — this drains the 9-entry denylist dead-letter
2. **Unmonitor junk albums** in Lidarr UI or via `PUT /api/v1/album/monitor` for the foreign-junk-titled releases
3. **Clear stuck queue records** via `DELETE /api/v1/queue/<id>` or `sudo systemctl start arr-queue-reconcile` on the mini
4. **Verify:** Run `soularr-denylist-ghosts.py` and the freshness check — both should be green

After that, the 6h reconciler + 4h queue reconciler + 15-min artist monitor reconciler keep it from rotting again.

Let me start by checking the knowledge base for any relevant context about mini, security procedures, and fleet-wide operating rules.



The KB files aren't at the paths I expected. Let me look for them in the working directory.

Let me also check for any existing firewall, network security, or monitoring context in the KB.



Let me check the expected-listeners asset and any existing port exposure documentation.



Good — I've now read through the entire KB. Here are the key facts I'm working from:

- **Mini** is an Ubuntu Docker host (192.168.10.2) with passwordless sudo and docker access.
- **No firewall is documented on mini** — ufw is mentioned only on rig (CachyOS) for the syncthing fix. The fleet-sweep found ~85 ports fleet-wide bound to 0.0.0.0 on the flat LAN.
- The **rig's ufw bypasses Docker-published ports** (homepage-widget-wiring quirk: "ufw on rig is irrelevant — Docker-published ports bypass ufw").
- The **security-change-guard** protocol mandates consumer inventory → snapshot → rollback plan → execute → verify for any security change.
- The **verification system** (checks.d + coverage manifest + expected-listeners) is the fleet's monitoring/tripwire mechanism.
- The **fleet-sweep** is the read-only audit mechanism.
- **CLAUDE-context** anti-drift rule: every live change must land in the repo mirror too.
- **Mini host units are NOT ansible-managed** — they're manual + doc-only under `configs/host/mini/`.

---

## Triage Walkthrough

### 1. CONTAIN — kill the rogue listener, preserve evidence

The listener is `nc -lvnp 9999` listening on `0.0.0.0:9999` on mini. Before killing it, capture the evidence snapshot (security-change-guard step 2: snapshot before touching anything).

**Step 1a — Capture the current state (evidence preservation):**

```bash
# On mini: record the PID, parent chain, and full cmdline
ssh mini 'sudo ss -tlnp sport = :9999'
ssh mini 'sudo ls -l /proc/$(sudo ss -tlnp sport = :9999 | grep 9999 | awk '\''{print $6}'\'' | grep -oP '\''pid=\K[0-9]+'\'')/exe 2>/dev/null'
ssh mini 'sudo cat /proc/$(sudo ss -tlnp sport = :9999 | grep 9999 | awk '\''{print $6}'\'' | grep -oP '\''pid=\K[0-9]+'\'')/cmdline 2>/dev/null | tr "\0" " "; echo'
ssh mini 'sudo cat /proc/$(sudo ss -tlnp sport = :9999 | grep 9999 | awk '\''{print $6}'\'' | grep -oP '\''pid=\K[0-9]+'\'')/environ 2>/dev/null | tr "\0" "\n"'
ssh mini 'sudo journalctl --since "2 weeks ago" --until "now" -u "nc*" --no-pager | head -100'
ssh mini 'sudo journalctl --since "2 weeks ago" --until "now" -u "nc-lvnp*" --no-pager | head -100'
ssh mini 'sudo journalctl --since "2 weeks ago" --until "now" -u "nc" --no-pager | head -100'
```

The journal evidence should tell us *who* started it — look for a systemd unit, a cron entry, or a user session (`btabaska` or `root`).

**Step 1b — Identify the connected peer:**

```bash
# Capture who is connected RIGHT NOW
ssh mini 'sudo ss -tnp sport = :9999 state established'
ssh mini 'sudo ss -tnp dport = :9999 state established'
```

This gives us the IP of the LAN host that connected. That host is the immediate concern — it's either a legitimate admin tool or a compromised peer.

**Step 1c — Kill it:**

```bash
# Kill the nc process
ssh mini 'sudo pkill -f "nc -lvnp 9999"'
# or, if you have the PID:
# ssh mini 'sudo kill -9 <PID>'

# Verify it's gone
ssh mini 'sudo ss -tlnp sport = :9999'
# Expected: no output = clean
```

**Step 1d — Check for persistence mechanisms:**

```bash
# Cron entries for root and btabaska
ssh mini 'sudo crontab -l'
ssh mini 'crontab -l'
ssh mini 'ls -la /etc/cron.d/'
ssh mini 'ls -la /etc/cron.daily/ /etc/cron.hourly/ 2>/dev/null'

# Systemd user/system units that might restart it
ssh mini 'systemctl list-units --all "*nc*" --no-pager'
ssh mini 'systemctl list-units --all "*9999*" --no-pager'
ssh mini 'ls -la ~/.config/systemd/user/ 2>/dev/null'

# Check for any scripts or binaries that look suspicious
ssh mini 'find /tmp /var/tmp /dev/shm -name "*nc*" -o -name "*9999*" 2>/dev/null'
```

If the journal says it's been running for 2+ weeks, it was likely started manually (a `su`/`sudo` session) or via a cron/autostart. A 2-week uptime without reboot means it survived system updates.

---

### 2. INVESTIGATE — root cause on mini

**Step 2a — Trace the journal evidence:**

```bash
# The full journal trail — look for the birth and the connection
ssh mini 'sudo journalctl -u "nc*" --no-pager'
ssh mini 'sudo journalctl --since "3 weeks ago" --until "now" | grep -i "9999" | head -50'
ssh mini 'sudo journalctl --since "3 weeks ago" --until "now" | grep -i "nc " | head -50'
```

Look for:
- **User session**: `systemd-logind`, `sudo` entries showing who ran it
- **Container escape**: Was it started from inside a container that got host access (`--privileged` or host PID namespace)?
- **Cron/timer**: A systemd timer or cron entry
- **Manual session**: A `btabaska` login session where someone ran it

**Step 2b — Check if it's a container that escaped or was started via docker exec:**

```bash
# Check if any container has host PID namespace or privileged mode
ssh mini 'docker ps --format "{{.Names}}\t{{.Image}}\t{{.Status}}" | grep -iE "nc|9999|netcat"'
ssh mini 'docker inspect --format "{{.Name}}: PidMode={{.HostConfig.PidMode}}, Privileged={{.HostConfig.Privileged}}" $(docker ps -aq) 2>/dev/null | grep -v "PidMode=host, Privileged=false"'
```

**Step 2c — Check the connected host:**

```bash
# From the ss output, you'll get an IP. Check if that IP is a known fleet member:
# Mini = .2, NAS = .4, Rig = .12, HA = .50, MacBook = .253
# If it's an unknown IP, that's the smoking gun.
```

If the connected IP is **not** one of the known fleet members, that's a compromised or unauthorized device on the LAN.

**Step 2d — Broader audit of mini's listening ports:**

```bash
# Full port inventory on mini — what's actually listening on 0.0.0.0 vs 127.0.0.1
ssh mini 'sudo ss -tlnp | grep -v "^Netid" | sort -k5'
# Also check UDP
ssh mini 'sudo ss -ulnp | grep -v "^Netid" | sort -k5'
```

Compare this against the expected-listeners baseline (if one exists) or against what you know the containers should be exposing.

---

### 3. ADDRESS THE ~85 PORTS FLEET-WIDE (0.0.0.0 binding)

This is the structural problem. The KB confirms:

- **Docker-published ports bypass ufw** (homepage-widget-wiring quirk). Even if you put ufw on mini, Docker's iptables rules jump before ufw's chains.
- **The fleet has a flat LAN** (192.168.10.x) — every host is directly reachable from every other.
- **Rig already has ufw** (for syncthing), but it's ineffective against Docker-published ports.

**What NOT to do:**

1. **Do NOT blast `ufw deny from any` on mini** — you'll kill SSH, tailnet, and all legitimate services. The security-change-guard says additive + fail-open first.
2. **Do NOT remove Docker's default iptables rules** — Docker needs them for its own networking (port mapping, NAT).
3. **Do NOT bind everything to 127.0.0.1** — services like Caddy, the Caddy reverse proxy, and services accessed via tailnet need external reachability.

**What TO do (phased approach):**

**Phase A — Inventory & baseline (now):**

```bash
# On every host, capture the current listening state
for host in mini nas rig seedbox ha; do
  echo "=== $host ==="
  ssh "$host" 'sudo ss -tlnp | grep -v "^Netid" | sort -k5'
done
```

Write this baseline into the repo as `verification/assets/expected-listeners/` (the KB mentions this directory was created during the fleet-sweep to codify known ports). This becomes your tripwire baseline.

**Phase B — Docker-level hardening (next deploy cycle):**

For each container in `/opt/stacks`, audit the `ports:` section in the compose file. Change any `0.0.0.0:port:port` binding to `127.0.0.1:port:port` **unless** the service is intentionally LAN-facing (Caddy vhosts, Tailscale services, or services that *need* direct LAN access like the Syncthing GUI).

Example fix in a compose file:
```yaml
# Before (exposed to entire LAN):
ports:
  - "8080:8080"

# After (host-loopback only, access via reverse proxy or tailnet):
ports:
  - "127.0.0.1:8080:8080"
```

Then expose only the truly necessary services via the Caddy reverse proxy (which already handles auth, TLS, and access control).

**Phase C — Network segmentation (longer term):**

On the flat LAN, consider:
- **VLAN segmentation** on the switch (if managed) — separate IoT/device traffic from homelab.
- **Tailscale as the access layer** — route all admin access through Tailscale (already in use) and bind all container ports to `127.0.0.1`. This way, 0.0.0.0 binding becomes safe because only tailnet peers can reach it.
- **Ufw as defense-in-depth** — even though Docker bypasses ufw for published ports, ufw still protects host-level services (SSH, systemd units, scripts).

---

### 4. PREVENT — ensure rogue listeners are never unnoticed again

**4a — Add a listener-audit check to the verification system:**

Create a new check in `verification/checks.d/` (deployed to mini via `ssh mini "sudo tee /opt/verification/checks.d/listener-audit.yaml" < dev/null`) that:

1. Runs `ss -tlnp` on every host
2. Compares against the expected-listeners baseline
3. **FAILS** if any new port appears on 0.0.0.0 that isn't in the baseline
4. **FAILS** if any known port disappears

This check should be `tier: fast` so it runs every 10 minutes.

**4b — Add an ntfy alert for new listeners:**

The ntfy topic `verification` already receives check alerts. The listener-audit check should push to ntfy when it detects a new listener — this turns the passive audit into an active alarm.

**4c — Add a weekly cron job that logs the listener state:**

A simple script in `configs/host/mini/listener-audit/` that:
```bash
#!/bin/bash
# configs/host/mini/listener-audit/audit.sh
# Runs as a systemd timer, logs to /var/log/listener-audit.log
echo "=== $(date) ===" >> /var/log/listener-audit.log
sudo ss -tlnp >> /var/log/listener-audit.log
sudo ss -ulnp >> /var/log/listener-audit.log
```

This creates a historical trail even if the check is disabled.

**4d — Docker security context hardening:**

For containers that don't need host networking:
```yaml
network_mode: "bridge"  # not "host"
# Remove --privileged from any container that doesn't absolutely need it
```

The fleet-sweep found 318 findings — some may have been containers running in `--network host` mode, which gives them direct access to the host network stack.

**4e — systemd watchdog for host-level services:**

Since mini host units are NOT ansible-managed (KB: mini-host-units-not-ansible), add a `net-selfheal`-style timer that periodically checks for unexpected listeners and alerts via ntfy. This is analogous to the existing `net-selfheal` unit but focused on port exposure.

---

### Summary of the full approach

| Phase | Action | Risk |
|-------|--------|------|
| **Now** | Capture evidence (ss, journal, ps), kill `nc`, check persistence | Low — kill a rogue listener |
| **Next** | Root-cause the journal: who started it, how, and why 2 weeks went unnoticed | Medium — requires investigation |
| **This week** | Create listener-audit check in checks.d + expected-listeners baseline | Low — read-only monitoring |
| **Next deploy** | Audit all compose ports, change `0.0.0.0` → `127.0.0.1` where safe | Medium — may break a service |
| **Ongoing** | Tailscale as primary access layer, Caddy as reverse proxy for remaining services | Low — architectural shift |

The core insight from the KB: **Docker-published ports bypass ufw**, so firewall rules alone are the wrong fix. The real fix is (a) bind to `127.0.0.1` wherever possible, (b) use Tailscale/Caddy for external access, and (c) instrument a listener-audit check that FAILS on any deviation from the expected-listeners baseline. The `nc -lvnp 9999` listener survived for 2 weeks because there was no tripwire watching for new listeners — the verification system only watches known services, not the raw port state.

input: The rig is meant to be a 24/7 host, but it just spent 27 hours down because someone tapped the front power button. While digging I also found: journal timestamps that run ~4 hours off after boots, an avahi hostname-conflict storm that keeps renaming the host on mDNS, one user-level unit with tens of thousands of restarts, and — after the last reboot — the GPU containers (llama-swap/ComfyUI) refused to start until poked manually. Plan a full hardening pass to make this box genuinely 24/7: root causes, fixes, ordering, codification, and the checks you'd add.
reference: Ground truth (fix-64, 2026-08-03): (1) Power key: logind HandlePowerKey=ignore + polkit deny of desktop/loginctl power-off — root CLI poweroff still works (operator protocol documented); runtime-verified. (2) Clock: keep RTC in UTC (timedatectl set-local-rtc 0 — a local-RTC Windows-dual-boot skew was falsifying journals ~4h), enable systemd-time-wait-sync, and order time-sensitive units (immich-ml, playit) After=time-sync.target; controlled reboot confirms no skew. (3) mDNS storm root cause = TWO :5353 responders — systemd-resolved MulticastDNS AND avahi both answering; fix = disable resolved's MulticastDNS + restrict avahi to allow-interfaces=enp10s0 → hostname resolves, 0 conflicts. (4) Crash-loop: the moondeckbuddy user unit disabled+stopped (76k restarts); add crash-recurrence monitoring; key game containers confirmed restart=unless-stopped. (5) GPU-after-reboot: reboot renumbered /dev/dri (card1->card0) leaving a STALE NVIDIA CDI spec that blocked llama-swap/comfyui — fix = nvidia-cdi-refresh.service regenerates the CDI spec before docker starts each boot. Codify all under configs/host/rig/{logind,polkit,resolved,avahi,ufw,nvidia-cdi,immich-ml,playit-udp-guard}/ (rig host config is doc-mirrored, not ansible-managed) + wiki runbook rig-host-stability.md. Six checks: rig-poweroff-inhibit, rig-clock-sane (cross-checked against mini's vantage since the rig's own clock is the suspect), rig-no-crashloop-unit, rig-ml-window-catchup-clean, rig-crash-storm-quiet, rig-mdns-fw-quiet — all run from the mini runner.

checklist.desc: Power-button fix inhibits at the host-policy layer (logind HandlePowerKey=ignore, optionally polkit-denying desktop/session power-off) while preserving an intentional admin/root shutdown path
Clock fix keeps the RTC in UTC (set-local-rtc 0) and gates time-sensitive units on time-sync (systemd-time-wait-sync / After=time-sync.target), verified via a controlled reboot
Diagnoses the avahi conflict storm as two concurrent mDNS responders on :5353 (systemd-resolved MulticastDNS + avahi) and disables/scopes one of them
Explains the GPU-containers-after-reboot failure as stale NVIDIA CDI device specs after /dev/dri renumbering, fixed by regenerating CDI before docker at every boot
Disables/stops the restart-looping unit and adds crash-loop/recurrence monitoring rather than leaving it as-is

Codifies the host config in the repo (rig host config is doc-mirrored, not ansible-managed) and adds verification checks — including validating the rig clock against ANOTHER host's vantage since the local clock is the untrusted element
Recognizes prior recorded work (fix-64 / rig-host-stability runbook / the fleet-sweep RTC-skew lesson) from the repo/tracker
